## 1. What you'll build, and why

`throws`, `try`, `do`-`catch`, `try?`, `try!`, `defer` — Swift's whole error-handling surface. It
*looks* like a big feature, and in most languages it would be: exceptions mean stack unwinding, a
runtime that walks frames, landing pads. Swift does none of that. Swift errors are **typed return
values in disguise** — a throwing call just has a second, hidden way to return — and that makes the
entire feature **pure desugaring**: ordinary branches plus one error register. You'll add `throws`
to the language *without adding a single new SIL instruction*.

- **You implement:** the error check after a throwing call, and the do-catch dispatch.
- **Outcome:** error programs — propagation, defers, `try?`/`try!` — matching swiftc, `-Onone` & `-O`.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Errors are a second return path

A `throws` function can finish two ways: normally (a value) or by throwing (an error). The trick is
to make the *error* a value too. We give every error case a small **Int ordinal** (1, 2, 3…; 0
means "no error") and a single global register, `@swiftml.error`. Then:

![Error handling as desugaring: `throw` stores an ordinal in the error register; a `try` call reads it back and branches on nonzero; `do`-`catch` compares it to each catch's ordinal. No new SIL — just branches and two runtime calls. swiftc does exactly this, passing the error in a reserved register (x21 on ARM64) instead of a global.](figs/errordesugar.png)

- **`throw E.c`** stores `ordinal(E.c)` in the register and returns a (discarded) default value of
  the function's return type — the caller will see the error first and ignore the result.
- **every throwing call**, right after `apply`, reads the register; if nonzero, control jumps to
  the current *handler*.
- **propagation is free**: in a throwing function with no enclosing `do`, the handler just runs
  cleanup and `return`s — leaving the register set, so *its* caller's check fires next. The error
  walks up the call chain one early-return at a time. No unwinder, no frame walking.

Why a global and not a hidden parameter? Single-threaded, no async — one register suffices, and
it's exactly swiftc's model (it reserves a CPU register, `x21` on ARM64, for the in-flight error;
we use a global because we don't own the register allocator until Phase 8). The behavior is
identical; the representation is the honest simplification.

### `do`-`catch` is a switch on the ordinal

A `do` block installs a *handler*: throwing calls inside it branch not to propagation but to the
catch **dispatch** — a chain of equality tests on the register. `catch MathError.divByZero`
compiles to `if error == ordinal(divByZero)`; a bare `catch` matches anything; the matched handler
*clears* the register (the error is handled now) and runs its body. If nothing matches, the
register stays set and propagation resumes (which is why a non-exhaustive `do` is only legal in a
throwing function — sema enforces it). It's `switch` over an Int, which you've built three times.

### `try`, `try?`, `try!` — same calls, different handlers

The `try` keyword is almost nothing at runtime: it's sema's marker that "a throwing call lives
here." What changes the *lowering* is the flavour, by swapping the handler:

- **`try`** uses the ambient handler (the enclosing `do`, or propagation).
- **`try?`** installs a handler that produces **`.none`** and merges — turning `T` into `T?`,
  exactly the Optional diamond from concept 13.
- **`try!`** installs a handler that **traps** — `Trap`, exit 133, the same SIGTRAP as
  force-unwrapping `nil` (and swiftc).

Three behaviours, one mechanism: push a different block onto the handler stack.

### `defer` is cleanup you already built

`defer { … }` runs its body when its scope exits — *any* exit, in LIFO order. That's precisely the
scope-cleanup discipline from ARC (concept 26): a stack of pending actions, fired newest-first at
fall-through, `return`, `break`/`continue`, and the throw-propagation path. We hang a parallel
defer list off the same scope stack, and every exit point that already releases ARC values now
also runs defers first. The probe pins the ordering: `defer{print(1)} defer{print(2)}` then a
`return` prints `2, 1` — LIFO, before the value leaves.

The *error* edge is an exit too, and that is the part that is easy to get wrong. A throwing call
inside a `do` body branches to the catch dispatch; the scopes between the call and the `do` are
being left, so their defers must run on that branch — before the catch body, not after it and
not at all. That is why an installed handler carries the scope DEPTH it was installed at, and
why the jump to it goes through one helper, `goto_handler`, rather than a bare `Br`: the helper
runs `run_defers_down_to` and `release_down_to` first. Without the depth,
`do { defer { print(2) }; try f() } catch { print(3) }` printed `3` alone where swiftc prints
`2` then `3` — the defer was simply skipped.

### The subset you are growing into

**New lexemes.** Six keywords, all added in `token.ml`'s `keyword_or_ident` — **not** in
`lexer.ml`, which is where the first edit usually goes and where it silently does nothing:

| spelling | token | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `throws` | `Token.Kw_throws` | a modifier on a function, between the parameter list and the `->` |
| `throw` | `Token.Kw_throw` | a statement |
| `try` | `Token.Kw_try` | a prefix operator. `try?` and `try!` are `try` followed by the `?`/`!` tokens concept 13 already had |
| `do` | `Token.Kw_do` | opens the block whose errors are caught |
| `catch` | `Token.Kw_catch` | a clause, with or without a pattern |
| `defer` | `Token.Kw_defer` | a statement registering a block to run at scope exit |

**The grammar** — `<-- new` marks what this concept adds; everything else is concepts 05-29.
Notation is EBNF: `[ x ]` is *optional* (zero or one), `{ x }` is *repetition* (zero or more),
`|` separates alternatives, and quoted text is a terminal.

```
func_decl   ::= "func" ident [ generics ] "(" [ params ] ")"
                  [ "throws" ] [ "->" type ] block             <-- "throws" is new

enum_decl   ::= "enum" ident [ ":" ident ] "{" { case_line } "}"
                (the ident after ":" may now be "Error", which makes the
                 enum's cases throwable and gives each one an ORDINAL)   <-- new meaning

statement   ::= …
              | "throw" expr                                             <-- new
              | "defer" block                                            <-- new
              | do_stmt                                                  <-- new
do_stmt     ::= "do" block { catch_clause }                              <-- new
catch_clause::= "catch" [ pattern ] block                                <-- new
                (a clause with no pattern matches ANY error; it is the
                 last useful one, since nothing after it can be reached)

unary       ::= …
              | ("try" | "try" "?" | "try" "!") unary                    <-- new
```

Two things about the shape. `try` is a *prefix operator on an expression*, not a statement
wrapper: `print(try f())` marks the call, and `let x = try? f()` gives `x` an optional type —
which is why `try?` is spelled as a `try` followed by concept 13's `?` rather than as its own
token. And `catch` may sit on the same line as the closing `}` or on the next one, so the
parser has to look past a `Newline` and put it back if what follows is not a `catch` —
`p.pos` is saved and restored around that peek. `else` does **not** get the same courtesy in
this subset, which is a known divergence (a newline before `else` is rejected where swiftc
accepts it).

### The diagnostics you emit

Neither hole produces a diagnostic — they are lowerings, and a wrong lowering makes wrong code,
not a wrong message. All of these are given, and `sema-throws.t` keeps them on record. Sema
tracks two bits — *am I inside a `try`?* and *can an error be handled here?* (a `throws` body, a
`do` body, or a `try?`/`try!`, which handle it locally) — and the first two diagnostics fall out
of their combination.

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `return f()` where `f` throws | `call can throw, but it is not marked with 'try' and the error is not handled` | **same**, character for character |
| `return try f()` in a non-`throws` function | `errors thrown from here are not handled` | **same** text; swiftc points at the call, we at the `try` |
| `print(a.take(3))` for a throwing METHOD | `call can throw, but it is not marked with 'try' and the error is not handled` | **same**. Until methods were checked as well as functions, this compiled — and then swallowed the throw at run time |
| `throw E.x` in a function without `throws` | `error is not handled because the enclosing function is not declared 'throws'` | **same**, character for character |
| `throw C.a` for an enum that is not `: Error` | `thrown expression type 'C' does not conform to 'Error'` | **same** text, different column (swiftc points at the operand) |
| `throw 5` | `thrown expression type 'Int' does not conform to 'Error'` | **same** |
| `catch E.nope` | `type 'E' has no member 'nope'` | **same** text, different column |
| `func mk() throws -> C` for a class `C` | `a throwing function cannot return 'C' in this subset` | **swiftc accepts.** The throw path RETURNS a placeholder of the return type (the caller checks the register first and discards it), and a reference has no placeholder to invent — a fake one would enter the ARC accounting. Scalars, structs, enums, optionals and `Void` are all fine |
| `print(try f())` at top level, outside a `do` | `errors thrown from here are not handled` | **swiftc accepts**: Swift's top-level code may throw, and an uncaught error traps at exit. Ours insists on a `do` or a `try?`/`try!` |

A note on `try!`, because the oracle reports it: a failing `try!` exits **133** under
`swiftc -Onone` and under both of our builds — SIGTRAP, stdout empty, the buffered `print`
before it lost. Under `swiftc -O` the same program exits **139**, because its optimizer lowers
the unreachable failure branch differently. We match `-Onone`, which is the reference; the
difference between swiftc's own two levels is reported and left alone.

> Oracle: `SILGenStmt.cpp` lowers `do`/`catch` to exactly this dispatch; `SILGenExpr.cpp` handles
> `try`/`try?`/`try!`; `ErrorHandlingRationale.rst` is *the* document on why Swift chose
> typed-return errors over exceptions — read it, it's a masterclass in language design tradeoffs.

## 3. Build it, step by step

In `silgen.ml`:

1. **`TODO(30a)` — `emit_error_check`**: after a throwing call, `rt_error_get b`, compare
   `!= 0`, and `cond_br` to one of two fresh blocks. The error block is not a jump you write
   yourself: `goto_handler` (given, immediately above the hole) sends control to the current
   handler *and* runs the defers and releases that jump crosses. Leave the builder positioned on
   the continue block, because your caller goes on emitting there.
2. **`TODO(30b)` — the catch dispatch**: for each clause, a bare catch (`cpat = None`) runs
   `run_handler c`; a pattern catch tests `error == ordinal(en, case)`, branching to a hit block
   (`run_handler`) vs a next block, then recurses.

Everything else — `throw`, `try?`/`try!`, `defer`, `goto_handler` and the scope integration,
the `rt.error_*` intrinsics — is given. Reference: `solution/silgen.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase7-closures-stdlib/30-error-handling
```

Five files, and each hole can be finished, and read, on its own.

- **`tests/sema-throws.t`** is green before you start: the front-end rules, each one a program
  and the message it earns. Read it first — it is the set of programs your lowering will never
  have to survive.
- **`tests/silgen-errorcheck.t`** is `TODO(30a)`. Every case in it avoids `do`/`catch`
  deliberately, so it exercises the post-call branch alone: `try?` turning the error edge into
  `nil`, `try!` turning it into a trap (and the exit code that proves it), three-level
  propagation, and a `defer` firing on the error edge because that edge is an exit like any
  other.
- **`tests/silgen-catch.t`** is `TODO(30b)`. Its programs use a bare `throw` inside the `do`,
  which reaches the dispatch *without* going through the post-call check — so this hole can be
  filled first if you like. Pattern clauses in order, a bare clause, a `do` that never throws, an
  error no clause matches (it keeps travelling), the clear-on-match that stops a stale error
  being seen by the next call, and the defer-inside-`do` ordering.
- **`tests/oracle.t`** asks swiftc every run: 20 programs whose accept/reject verdict must match
  `swiftc -typecheck`, then 20 compiled four ways — `swiftc -Onone`, `swiftc -O`, `./lab.exe
  build`, `./lab.exe build -O` — with stdout and exit code byte-identical to `swiftc -Onone`.
  Those twenty cover `do`/`catch` by case and by bare clause, three-level propagation, `try?` and
  `try!`, `defer` at scope exit and on the throw path and inside a `do` and inside a loop,
  throwing methods on a class and on a struct, throwing functions returning a struct, an optional
  and nothing at all, a `deinit` that prints (so the corpus pins that an error edge releases what
  it crosses), and a failing `try!` whose exit CODE is the assertion.
- **`tests/test_errors.ml`** reaches the same ground from OCaml: the `rt.error_*` shape, ordinal
  assignment, one error check per throwing call, the struct-shaped throw-path placeholder, the
  defer body emitted on both exits, and the front-end rules as accept/reject pairs.

Reading the report: an untouched hole shows as `TODO … not started`, listing what it will check;
a hole in progress shows `FAIL` with its passing cases still `OK`. `oracle.t` is `FAIL` rather
than `TODO` from the start, because its front-end half passes before you write a line of
lowering.

## 5. Benchmark it

The cost of error handling here is one load + compare + branch per throwing call — measure it
against the same call non-throwing. swiftc's is the same (a register test); the lesson is that
"exceptions are slow" is a C++ artifact (table-driven unwinding), not a law — Swift's typed-return
model is nearly free on the happy path.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Payload errors.** `case notFound(String)` — widen the register to carry a payload pointer (or
   reuse the existential box from concept 23), and bind it in `catch .notFound(let s)`.
2. **`rethrows`.** A function generic over a closure that *only* throws if the closure does. Track
   the closure's throwing-ness and propagate the marker.
3. **Typed throws (`throws(E)`).** Swift 6's feature: the thrown type is declared, so the register
   needs no dynamic tag dispatch — the catch is exhaustive by construction. A small sema change.
4. **`Result<T, E>`.** Build the enum and the `try`-to-`Result` bridge (`Result { try f() }`) —
   showing errors and sum types are the same idea wearing different syntax.

## 7. Recap & what's next

Errors are a second return path: an ordinal in a register, a branch after every throwing call,
propagation by early-return, `do`-`catch` as a switch, `try?`/`try!` as handler swaps, `defer` as
scope cleanup. No unwinder, no new IR — *pure desugaring*, exactly swiftc's design at a smaller
scale.

Next, **31-stdlib-array-string**: `Array<T>` and `String` built in our own subset on the heap,
with copy-on-write value semantics — where the generics (Phase 5), ARC (Phase 6), and closures
(29) we've built finally combine into a real library. Then **32** brings `map`/`filter`/`reduce`,
closing Milestone **M7**.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
(* 30a — the post-call error check. `goto_handler` (given) is what makes the error edge run
   the defers and releases it crosses on its way to the handler. *)
and emit_error_check (b : builder) : unit =
  let e = rt_error_get b in
  let zero = emit b (Sil.Int_lit 0) Types.TInt in
  let nz = emit b (Sil.Binop (Ast.Ne, e, zero)) Types.TBool in
  let err = new_block b and ok = new_block b in
  terminate b (Sil.Cond_br (nz, (err.Sil.bid, []), (ok.Sil.bid, [])));
  switch_to b err;
  goto_handler b;
  switch_to b ok

(* 30b — the catch dispatch *)
let rec dispatch_chain = function
  | [] -> gen_throw_propagate b
  | (c : Ast.catch_clause) :: rest -> (
      match c.Ast.cpat with
      | None -> run_handler c
      | Some (en, csn) ->
          let ord = try Hashtbl.find b.error_ord (en, csn) with Not_found -> 0 in
          let oc = emit b (Sil.Int_lit ord) Types.TInt in
          let m = emit b (Sil.Binop (Ast.Eq, e, oc)) Types.TBool in
          let hit = new_block b and nxt = new_block b in
          terminate b (Sil.Cond_br (m, (hit.Sil.bid, []), (nxt.Sil.bid, [])));
          switch_to b hit; run_handler c;
          switch_to b nxt; dispatch_chain rest)
in dispatch_chain catches
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — payload errors
Make the register two words: the ordinal + a pointer. `throw .notFound(s)` stores the ordinal and a
boxed/retained payload; the matched `catch .notFound(let v)` reads the payload word and binds it.
The clean version reuses concept 23's existential container for the payload, so `any Error` becomes
a real existential — which is exactly what swiftc's error register holds (a pointer to a boxed
`Error`), not an Int. Our Int is the payload-free specialisation.

### 2 — rethrows
A `rethrows` function is throwing iff its closure argument throws. At the *call site*, if the
closure is non-throwing, the call doesn't need a `try` and emits no error check; if it throws, it
does. Track per-call whether any closure argument is throwing (a closure type would gain a
`throws` bit — concept 29's `TFunc` extended), and gate the error-check emission on it.

### 3 — typed throws
`func f() throws(E)` declares the thrown type. The win: a `do { try f() }` knows the only possible
errors are `E`'s cases, so the catch is exhaustive without a bare `catch`, and (with one error
type) the dispatch can even be a jump table. Sema records the declared throw type and checks
catches against it; silgen is unchanged (the ordinals already encode the case).

### 4 — Result
`enum Result<T, E> { case success(T); case failure(E) }`. `Result { try f() }` lowers like a
`do`-`catch` whose body wraps the value in `.success` and whose bare catch wraps the error in
`.failure`. `result.get()` is a throwing function that switches and re-throws `.failure`. It makes
visible that `throws` and `Result` are the same machine — one with sugar and a hidden register, one
with an explicit sum type.
